name: Ivan Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ivan, 43, and I'm still the junior one carrying cable in before the supervisor checks where we start. I took a vocational certificate last year after packing work became patchy, and I'm slower at wiring and repairs than the experienced electricians. My partner Ema works part-time in a school kitchen; we have two children, ten and thirteen, and a mortgage. My pay is low, the days can vary, and we've got less than two weeks of expenses saved, so a quiet afternoon at work isn't always restful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I'm glad the argument can quieten down because I'm still trying to learn the ordinary job. A customer wants the lights working, not my opinion about machines. I'd ask the supervisor to show me the next task clearly and let me get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI doing little wouldn't fix our money. I'm 43, new to this trade and earning a junior wage, with less than two weeks of expenses saved. Some weeks the paid hours vary, and the mortgage is the same size every month. There aren't many other electrical firms nearby if this one stops giving me enough days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep doing the supervised wiring and repair tasks I'm given, rather than leave a paid job on a worry. This week I'd ask the supervisor to write down my expected days for the coming month so my partner and I can plan the mortgage payment. During the first year I'd keep checking that calendar with my partner every Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a short week already means moving bills around. I'm relieved the trade itself isn't changing overnight in this picture. That doesn't make the kitchen-table sums any nicer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you come into electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I moved from packing work after it became too patchy and finished a vocational certificate last year. I'm still slower than the other electricians and need the supervisor to check what I do. Starting again wasn't supposed to be easy, but I'd hoped it would become steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which payment do you plan around first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, then food and the basic bills. My partner Ema works part-time in a school kitchen, and we have two children, ten and thirteen. My partner's wage helps, but it doesn't replace my paid days.

say: I'd welcome fewer **machine arguments** while I learn the ordinary electrical tasks properly.
I'd ask the **supervisor** for clear instructions rather than offer customers opinions about AI.
think: My **junior wage** and variable paid days already make the mortgage difficult to plan.
I have under **two weeks saved** and few nearby employers if this job stops providing enough days.
do: Keep doing **supervised wiring** and repairs rather than leave paid work because of worry.
Request a written **days calendar** this week and review it with my partner every Sunday.
feel: **Anxious** about short working weeks, despite relief that the trade isn't changing radically.
S0.quote: Some weeks the paid hours vary, and the mortgage is the same size every month.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** concerns variable junior earnings, a mortgage and two children, not a fabricated immediate automation loss.
The **vocational certificate** follows a recent career change; he remains below-average and supervised rather than being assigned a licence or senior duties.

steps.text: Keep supervised wiring tasks and review expected paid days with partner each Sunday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody needs to ask what the faster planning does to the people still learning. I don't use AI, and I wouldn't tell a customer I understood a system when I didn't. The company should give us proper paid time if it changes how the work is organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork might go first, but a tighter timetable could still cost me paid days. I'm the slow junior who needs another check, so I worry the owner would choose a quicker worker for the shorter route. I don't think the cables disappear; I'm worried about which person gets sent to pull them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a union representative this month about joining and attend the next workers' meeting on paid learning time. At work I'd keep a paper record of my assigned jobs and the paid hours, asking the supervisor to check it each Friday. During the first year I'd use that record in discussions about hours rather than pretend I could operate the new planning system unaided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit ashamed of being the slow one at my age. Talking with other workers would make it less like a private failure. I still wouldn't want a meeting to turn into promising each other the jobs can't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the workers' meeting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clear request that required training happens in paid time, with someone showing us the actual steps. I'd join that request rather than sign a paper I hadn't read. I'm not asking the representative to promise the owner will agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you handle unfamiliar tools today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wait for the supervisor to show me, then do the same steps again on paper if I need to remember. I've never used an AI tool. I don't want my first attempt to be on a customer's wiring or a form I don't understand.

say: I'd ask how faster **planning** affects workers who are still learning.
I'd say required **training** should happen in paid time with someone showing the actual steps.
think: A tighter **timetable** could cost me days because I'm slower and need extra checks.
I worry about **who gets sent** to do physical work, not cables disappearing into software.
do: Ask about **union membership** and join the request for paid learning time at the next meeting.
Keep a **paper record** of assigned jobs and paid hours, checked with the supervisor each Friday.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer paid days and embarrassed by needing help at 43.
S1.quote: I don't think the cables disappear; I'm worried about which person gets sent to pull them.
fieldNote: He links **planning automation** to assignment and income pressure while preserving the low thinking exposure of physical electrical tasks.
The **collective request** involves a meeting and shared demand, not merely individual teaching or a hoped-for entitlement.

steps.text: Join the union request for paid learning time at the next workers meeting
Keep supervised work and paper records of assigned jobs and paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the dates plainly: thinking AI in 2028 and robots doing hands-on work around 2031. I wouldn't tell the children that choosing a trade solves everything. I'd tell the crew we need a serious discussion about what happens to junior hours before anyone signs for a new van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the junior jobs like mine would lose a big share of paid hours once capable robots arrive, maybe before I've become a confident electrician. Thinking systems could squeeze my assignments earlier too. With the mortgage and almost no cash behind us, I'm already rehearsing the call to the lender when I should be asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd contact the mortgage lender now to ask what help exists if my paid days fall, without assuming I'd qualify. My partner and I would stop the monthly family takeaway this month to keep that money for bills. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid supervised work where offered, and take actual payslips to a free debt adviser if reduced earnings put us short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I'd expect a big hole in the household income when the robots follow. I can make the calls and keep turning up, but I don't see spare money for another fresh start. I hate imagining my children hearing me and my partner argue over a mortgage letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the lender on that first call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I earn now, that my days vary and that I want to understand the options before missing anything. I'd ask about eligibility, costs and what happens afterwards, then write the answer down. I wouldn't put a lower payment in our budget unless it had actually been agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the children hear from you instead of an argument?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children we're checking the bills and they haven't caused the problem. The older one has a school trip next year, and I wouldn't cancel it tonight just to show I'm frightened. We'd check the actual cost and the school's payment options before making a decision.

say: I'd explain **both dates** at home and avoid promising the children permanent safety in a trade.
I'd ask the **crew** to discuss junior hours before new spending commitments.
think: I expect a large **hours loss** once robots arrive, possibly before I'm confident in this new trade.
The **mortgage** and tiny reserve keep me awake, with earlier planning changes also threatening assignments.
do: Contact the **mortgage lender** now about eligibility and costs without assuming lower payments.
Stop the **monthly takeaway** this month and retain that money for bills.
Keep **paid supervised work** after 2028 and seek free debt advice with payslips if earnings leave us short.
feel: **Alarmed** about a large household income loss, while still able to make calls and keep working.
S2.quote: I hate imagining my children hearing me and my partner argue over a mortgage letter.
fieldNote: His **expected major loss** follows later robots; earlier assignments may shrink while physical work continues in the first post-2028 year.
The **lender inquiry** preserves eligibility, fees and actual agreement; neither reduced payments nor free advice is treated as guaranteed income.

steps.text: Ask the mortgage lender about support eligibility and costs before assuming any payment change
Stop the monthly family takeaway and retain the money for bills
Keep paid supervised electrical work after 2028 where offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people like me time to become useful if the firm will teach us properly. Thinking AI in 2031 is still followed by robots around 2034. I'd ask for paid training and honest hours, not a speech about how everyone must be positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, with children around fifteen and eighteen, so the household wouldn't simply stop needing my wages. I might be better at the job by then, but my days could still be cut before I've built any reserve. More years is a chance to learn, not money already in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor now about a practical wiring course and a written plan for supported practice. I'd enrol only if the firm covered fees and paid me for the class time; otherwise I'd keep supervised work and ask for practice within my existing paid day. In the first year after 2031 I'd use any completed training on paid jobs under the checks my supervisor still required.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less breathless than with the two-year date. I can picture finishing something useful rather than rushing to sign up for whatever appears first. I still have this month's mortgage to pay while I picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for the course if the firm refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't borrow for the course. A loan for a wiring course would need repaying whether the teaching got me more paid hours or not. I'd ask the union representative to include paid training in the workers' request instead. A plan that starts by taking money out of the food account isn't a plan I can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about careers to your older child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should look at what the child likes and what a course actually costs, rather than naming a supposedly safe job. I'd ask the school about advice and support when the choices come up. My own difficult restart doesn't mean I know the whole future.

say: I'd ask for **paid training** and honest hours rather than pressure to sound positive.
I'd explain that **five years** allows learning while robots still follow thinking AI around 2034.
think: At **48**, I'd still need wages for my household when thinking AI arrived in 2031.
My **paid days** could shrink before I build a reserve, even if more time improves my skills.
do: Request a **wiring course** now with supported practice agreed by the supervisor.
Enrol only with **fees covered** and paid class time, otherwise practise within my existing paid day.
Use any **completed training** on paid jobs after 2031 with required supervision.
feel: **Anxious** about present bills and paid days, with more room to complete useful learning.
S3.quote: A loan for a wiring course would need repaying whether the teaching got me more paid hours or not.
fieldNote: His **resistance** remains visible in wanting supported practical learning and familiar supervision rather than suddenly adopting AI or an unrelated career.
The **course commitment** requires funded fees and paid class time; extra years do not guarantee savings or higher paid hours.

steps.text: Enrol in the wiring course only with covered fees and paid class time
Keep supervised work and supported practice within paid hours if course funding is refused
Join the union paid-training request if employer course funding is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should be enough warning for employers to train people rather than blame them at the end. I'd tell the children we can talk through their choices, not promise a job that machines never touch. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still matter to a family like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when the thinking systems arrived and about 56 when the robots followed. I don't have a pension or a paid-off mortgage I can count on then, so I still need to earn. The extra time reduces the rush about AI, but our present short weeks and thin savings still make me anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep asking for the funded, paid-time wiring course now and continue supervised work if the firm refused. My partner and I would review the next month's paid days and mortgage money on the last Sunday of each month. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid electrical work where offered and ask the lender or adviser about real options if the household fell short, rather than assume I could retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slower, more ordinary way. Thinking AI arriving in 2036 lets me breathe about machines but doesn't put extra days on this month's payslip. I'd like time to help the children without every school letter becoming another sum I can't settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful employer promise look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written number of paid training hours and the course fees covered, with a named person showing me the practical steps. I'd rather read a small promise the owner actually agreed than a poster about lifelong learning. I'd keep asking through the workers' meeting if it wasn't offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the children to remember about this period?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we checked things together and didn't blame them for needing school shoes. My partner and I can be worried without making the children carry the mortgage. I'd still want them to ask questions when grown-ups claim a machine will fix every bill.

say: I'd say **ten years' warning** should support real training rather than later blame for workers.
I'd discuss the **children's choices** without promising an occupation that machines never touch.
think: I'll still need **earnings at 53**, without a pension or cleared mortgage I can safely count on.
Our current **short weeks** and thin reserve remain worrying even with less urgency around AI.
do: Seek the **funded wiring course** only with paid class time, continuing supervised work if refused.
Review **paid days** and mortgage money with my partner on each month's last Sunday.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and request lender or advice options if actual household income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about current earnings and family bills, with less added urgency from distant automation.
S4.quote: Thinking AI arriving in 2036 lets me breathe about machines but doesn't put extra days on this month's payslip.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** softens automation urgency without erasing current financial strain, changing his junior status today or guaranteeing pension access later.
He specifies **paid training hours**, covered fees and a named teacher rather than treating a vague learning promise as usable help.

steps.text: Enrol in wiring training only with employer-covered fees and paid class time
Keep supervised work and review paid days with partner each month
Ask lender or adviser about actual options if income falls short after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a big loss of junior hours when robots follow around 2031, without enough cash to carry us. Paid practical training, clear paid days and advice about real mortgage options would help. I'd want workers involved in those decisions rather than each family being told to manage alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person starting again at 43 has anybody patient enough to teach them. I can learn a trade, but I can't ask my children to pause growing while I learn it. I don't use AI and I'd rather say that honestly than pretend I'm already comfortable.

headlineQuote: I can learn a trade, but I can't ask my children to pause growing while I learn it.
portrait: Ivan is **43**, a junior electrician with a recent vocational certificate, below-average skill and continuing supervision after leaving patchy packing work.
He has a **partner and two children**, a mortgage, low variable earnings and fewer than two weeks of expenses saved.
He has **never used AI** and seeks familiar practical instruction, union involvement and paid learning rather than unsupported technology experiments.
Fast AGI brings **expected junior-hours losses** and lender inquiries; longer horizons preserve current money worries and conditional course funding.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little cushion before he expects a major loss of junior hours when robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** and clear paid days would help him learn while meeting household bills.
Advice about **actual mortgage options** and workers' involvement would help families plan without assumed support entitlements.
